lead: A transition diagram is a flow chart that recognises one token class. Its circles are states; its arrows consume one input character each. The lexer starts at the start state, follows arrows labelled with the current character, and accepts at a double circle. These diagrams turn a regular expression into a step-by-step recogniser for identifiers, numbers, operators and keywords. A scanner uses them, or a table built from them, to cut source text into tokens for the parser.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for regular expressions and token patterns.

blocks.text: A state records how much of a token has been read. The start state is where every attempt begins. An accepting state is drawn as a double circle and marks a complete lexeme of that token class. A transition edge from state p to state q labelled c means: in state p, if the next character is c, consume it and move to q. If no edge carries the current character, the attempt fails. A diagram for a single rule recognises one token class. A scanner joins several rules into one diagram by branching from a common start state. It is not a parser and does not check grammar.

Labels use L for any letter, D for any digit, and _ for underscore. A label such as L, D, _ means any one of those characters. Some syllabi call these lexical transition diagrams. Read one by walking it: from the start state, each input character chooses one outgoing edge. Arriving at an accepting state means the characters read so far form a lexeme. The same diagram can be stored as a table, which is how a scanner program runs it.

sections.h3: Diagrams for identifiers, integers, operators and keywords

blocks.text: An identifier begins with a letter or underscore and continues with letters, digits or underscores. Start at q0. An edge labelled L or _ goes to q1. State q1 loops on L, D, _. State q1 is accepting. This accepts rate2 and _x, but not 2rate as one identifier.

An unsigned integer is simpler: q0 on any digit D goes to q2; q2 loops on D; q2 accepts. This accepts 0, 7 and 2024. Relational operators need branching. For <, <= and <>: q0 on < goes to q1. q1 on = goes to an accepting state for LE. q1 on > goes to an accepting state for NE. State q1 is itself accepting, for LT. The lexer backs up to q1 when the next character is not = or >.

A keyword such as if is a short chain: q0 on i to q1, q1 on f to accepting q2. A scanner may instead recognise an identifier and then look the spelling up in a keyword table. Figure combines identifier and integer recognition from one start state.

sections.h3: Longest match, backup and rule order

blocks.text: Try diagrams in a fixed order: longest match wins, then the earlier rule.

items: Set state to the start state and last_accept to none.
Read the next character. If an edge from the current state carries it, consume the character, move along the edge, and continue. Record the input position whenever the state is accepting.
When no edge carries the character, or input ends, stop.

If the current state is accepting, return the token ending at the current position. Otherwise return the token ending at last_accept and reset the input to just after that position. If there is no last_accept, report an error.

blocks.text: This rule is the longest match or maximal munch. It explains why rate2 is one identifier, not rate followed by 2, and why <= is one operator, not < then =. Order matters when two diagrams accept the same text. if matches both the keyword diagram and the identifier diagram. List keywords before identifiers, and longer operators before their prefixes. A combined diagram avoids some ordering: separate branches from one start state, and choose the accepting branch with the longest match.

figure.caption: One start state q0 splits into two token classes: a letter or underscore begins an identifier at accepting state q1, a digit begins a number at accepting state q2, and both accepting states loop on more letters or digits. Walking rate2 up the top branch stays in q1 until the space, where no edge leaves, so the lexer stops and emits ID(rate2).

spec.aria: State q0 branches on a letter or underscore to accepting state q1, which recognises rate2 as an identifier, or on a digit to accepting state q2, which recognises 2 as an unsigned integer; both accepting states loop on their allowed characters.

examples.question: Using the combined diagram in the figure, trace the input rate2 then a space then 2rate. List the tokens and the characters consumed.
steps: Start at q0 on r: a letter, so go to q1 and accept ID so far: r.
q1 loops on a, t, e and 2 because each is a letter or digit. After rate2, q1 is accepting.
Space has no edge from q1. Stop at the last accept, emit ID(rate2), and leave the space unread.
Skip the space and restart at q0. On 2 go to q2 and accept NUM so far: 2.
Next is r, which is not a digit. No edge from q2 carries r. Stop and emit NUM(2).
Restart at q0 on r go to q1; loop on a, t, e. Input ends in accepting q1, so emit ID(rate).

traps: An accepting state means a lexeme of that class is complete; it does not mean the whole input is valid.
Always take the longest accepting prefix, not the first accepting state. rate2 is ID(rate2), not ID(rate) then NUM(2).
On failure, back up to the last accepting state and leave the unread characters for the next token; do not discard the whole token.
Keywords must be tested before identifiers, and <= before <; otherwise the keyword and the two-character operator are lost.
A transition label consumes exactly one character; an edge labelled L does not consume a whole word.

quiz.q: What does a double circle mean in a transition diagram?
quiz.a: It is an accepting state: the characters read so far form a complete lexeme of that token class.

quiz.q: Why does a lexer need to back up to the last accepting state?
quiz.a: A longer path may fail after passing a shorter accepting prefix. Backup keeps the longest valid lexeme and leaves the extra characters for the next token.

quiz.q: Trace x1 on the combined diagram in the figure. Which token is produced?
quiz.a: q0 on x (letter) goes to q1; q1 on 1 (digit) loops to q1; q1 is accepting. Token is ID(x1).

quiz.q: Trace 12ab on the combined diagram. List the tokens.
quiz.a: q0 on 1 goes to q2; q2 on 2 loops to q2, accepting NUM(12). On a there is no digit edge, so emit NUM(12). Restart at q0 on a goes to q1; loop on b; emit ID(ab). Tokens: NUM(12), ID(ab).

quiz.q: Why must keyword diagrams be tried before the identifier diagram?
quiz.a: Every keyword is also a valid identifier. If the identifier rule runs first, if is returned as ID(if) and the keyword is never seen.

quiz.q: In the label L, D, _, what does each symbol allow?
quiz.a: L allows any letter, D any digit, and _ the underscore character; the label allows any one of them per transition.

quiz.q: Using the relational-operator diagram in the text, trace <= and <x.
quiz.a: Trace <=: q0 on < goes to q1; q1 on = goes to the accepting state for LE, so the token is LE. Trace <x: q0 on < goes to q1, which is accepting for LT; x has no edge from q1, so back up to q1 and accept LT, leaving x for the next token.

quiz.q: A diagram for <, <= and <> must look at the character after < to choose between LT, LE and NE. What goes wrong without backup?
quiz.a: After reading <, the lexer would need to inspect the next character to choose between LT, LE and NE. Without backup it must either consume that character or lose the ability to return LT; backup lets it return LT and leave the character unread.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real scanners compile many transition diagrams into one table-driven DFA, so one pass over the input handles all token classes. The longest-match rule is still called maximal munch in scanner generators such as flex. Modern scanners also handle Unicode letters, nested comments and very large files, sometimes with parallel or SIMD character classification. Search for maximal munch, table-driven lexical analysis and flex longest match to go further.
